content: It primarily evaluates the levels of ground-level ozone and particulate matter, excluding pollen counts. Various organizations worldwide calculate AQI values, but the definitions and classifications of air quality can vary between regions. In the United States, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) uses the following AQI classifications: An AQI of 0-50 is considered Good and is typically represented by the color green. An AQI of 51-100 is classified as Moderate and is usually shown in yellow. An AQI of 101-150 is labeled Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups and is represented in orange. An AQI of 151-200 is deemed Unhealthy and is shown in red. An AQI of 201-300 is categorized as Very Unhealthy and is represented in purple. An AQI of 301-500 is considered Hazardous and is shown in maroon. For reference, an AQI of 100 corresponds to an ozone concentration of 0.08 parts per million (ppm), with different thresholds for other pollutants. In Canada, the Meteorological Service of Canada (MSC) employs a more stringent AQI system. The classifications are as follows: An AQI of 0-25 is considered Good and is represented in green. An AQI of 26-50 is classified as Fair and is shown in yellow. An AQI of 51-100 is labeled Poor and is represented in orange. An AQI of 101 or higher is categorized as Very Poor and is shown in red. In Ontario, Canada, the AQI system is further refined. An AQI of 0-15 is classified as Very Good and is represented in blue. The upper limit for Good is 31, while 32 marks the lower limit for Moderate. In June 2007, the EPA proposed tightening the air pollution standards related to smog. This proposal followed recommendations from an independent scientific board, which stated that the existing standards were insufficient and lacked scientific justification. As a result, future adjustments to the AQI may reclassify pollution levels currently labeled as Moderate to Unhealthy. The AQI can worsen due to stagnant air conditions, which prevent the dispersion of pollutants. Such conditions are often caused by anticyclones, temperature inversions, or a lack of wind. Hong Kong In Hong Kong, the Air Pollution Index (API) is used to assess air quality. An API of 100 or below indicates pollutant levels that are satisfactory and pose no immediate health risks. An API exceeding 100 (Very High) indicates that pollutant levels are in the unhealthy range. Malaysia Malaysia uses the Air Pollution Index (API) to report air quality. Unlike the U.S. AQI, the Malaysian API can exceed 500. When this occurs, a state of emergency is declared in the affected area. During such emergencies, non-essential government services are suspended, ports are closed, and private sector activities (excluding the food sector) may be restricted. Singapore Singapore uses the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) to report air quality levels. United Kingdom The United Kingdom's Met Office provides air quality forecasts using an index ranging from 1 to 10 or descriptive bands (low, moderate, high, or very high). These levels are based on the health effects of specific pollutants. The forecasts include information on various pollutants and their associated health risks. United States The United States previously used the Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) to report air quality. However, it has since been replaced by the AQI, which is more sensitive. For instance, the AQI includes particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of less than 2.5 micrometers (PM2.5), replacing the less sensitive PM10 component of the PSI. Notes ppmv refers to parts per million by volume, indicating the volume of a pollutant gas per million volumes of ambient air. PM10 refers to particulate matter smaller than 10 micrometers in diameter. μg/m³ represents micrograms of a pollutant per cubic meter of ambient air. μm stands for micrometer. Over the past 23 years, air quality in the United States has significantly improved.
